AFDRAH

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
240 PM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* No major changes

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 240 PM Saturday...

1) A warm and humid day today, with afternoon showers and another 
round of showers/thunderstorms later tonight. 

2) Limited chances of a shower or storm Sunday afternoon and Sunday 
night, with the greatest chances during the afternoon across the 
Coastal Plain. 

3) A northeast flow will result in near average temperatures and 
lower humidity on Tuesday and Wednesday that will feel cooler than 
recent days.

4) The low and mid level flow will become more east and 
southeasterly late in the work week and weekend resulting in warming 
temperatures, an increase in humidity, and an uptick in rain 
chances. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 240 PM Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... A warm and humid day today, with afternoon showers 
and another round of showers/thunderstorms later tonight.

Last night into this morning, a boundary set up over central NC, 
bisecting the region in half. Shower activity started developing 
along this boundary as it started lifting north over Wake county 
just after noon. PWs over the region are very high (around 2-2.3 in) 
which will allow showers to be efficient rain producers this 
afternoon. This will combine with slow cell motions to create an 
isolated flooding threat, especially if a shower moves over an urban 
or poor drainage area. The area of any showers/thunderstorms should 
increase over the next few hours as the boundary continues north and 
outflows from previous showers/storms provides additional areas of 
lift. 

Later this evening into tonight, an additional area of 
shower/thunderstorm development may be possible as a pre-frontal 
trough moves through central NC from the west. Any rain that 
develops due to this should move faster than this afternoon's rain, 
leading to a lower flooding threat. 

In terms of the strength of the cells today, severe weather is not 
currently expected. CAPE values this afternoon look to maximize 
around 1500-2000 J/kg, with low shear values. This should allow for 
a few cells to get tall enough to produce lightning, but keep any 
winds with them below severe strength. However, a few water-loaded 
downdrafts could produce brief periods of strong gusty winds this 
afternoon. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Limited chances of a shower or storm Sunday 
afternoon and Sunday night, with the greatest chances during the 
afternoon across the Coastal Plain.

A mid level short wave trough across TN and AL at midday today will 
be located just east of the Blue Ridge on Sunday morning and then 
move offshore by Sunday evening. The best forcing for ascent will be 
east of this feature and should be exiting our eastern areas during 
the afternoon. Deep layer moisture will be above average areawide on 
Sunday but greatest across the east. Expect Sunday to be less 
convectively active than today with the greatest threat of a shower 
or storm across the east during the afternoon. However, a cold front 
will trail behind the short wave trough and move across the area 
late Sunday night and there is a limited chance or a shower or storm 
in the lingering moisture ahead of the front on Sunday night. Highs 
should range in the upper 80s to lower 90s with lows near 70. 


KEY MESSAGE 3... A northeast flow will result in near average 
temperatures and lower humidity on Tuesday and Wednesday that will 
feel cooler than recent days.

An anomalously strong mid-level ridge centered in the TN Valley on 
Tuesday and Wednesday will result in a northerly flow at mid levels 
across VA and the Carolinas while a 1030 mb surface high pressure 
system centered over New England will produce a northeast low level 
flow across the area. The result will be near to slightly above 
seasonal temperatures that will feel notably cooler than recent 
weeks. Highs should range in the lower to mid 80s both days and 
nighttime lows in the lower to mid 60s with some upper 50s (maybe 
mid 50s) possible in the typically cooler locations. Dry weather 
with partly cloudy skies and a noticeable northeast breeze at times 
are expected during the period. 


KEY MESSAGE 4... The low and mid level flow will become more east 
and southeasterly late in the work week and weekend resulting in 
warming temperatures, an increase in humidity, and an uptick in rain 
chances. 

The upper-level ridge at mid levels weakens late in the week and 
becomes more west to east oriented as a mid level weakness/upper low 
organizes near the Bahamas and shifts west into the northern Gulf. 
Meanwhile the narrow surface ridge extending southwest into VA and 
the Carolinas weakens late in the work week as a weak coastal front 
tries to develop off the Carolina coast. The result for our area 
will be an increase in temperatures, moisture and clouds and 
depending on the track and evolution of the upper low and coastal 
font, an uptick in rain chances over the weekend that could increase 
further early next week. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/... 
As of 145 PM Saturday...

As of the 17Z observations, there remains a mix of MVFR to VFR 
ceilings over central NC. Overnight, a boundary bisected the region, 
with sub-VFR ceilings in the north which have been generally slow to 
lift. This boundary will continue to shift north this afternoon, 
which will allow ceilings to continue to lift/scatter out, along 
with allowing a mechanism for isolated to scattered shower 
development. A few rumbles of thunder may be possible in these 
cells, but they should generally remain as rain showers with some 
gusty winds. Later this evening into the night, another chance for 
rain will come ahead of a cold front. Due to increased moisture and 
the approaching frontal boundary, there could be a period of IFR to 
perhaps LIFR ceilings and/or reduced visibilities late tonight/early 
Sunday morning. Restrictions may remain in place until the front 
moves through central NC Sunday afternoon. 

Outlook: There will be a limited risk of shower/storm development 
along the frontal passage Sunday afternoon into the evening. There 
is a lesser, but non-zero chance of low stratus and/or fog 
development again on Monday morning as well. VFR conditions are then 
generally expected to prevail. 

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...Blaes/LH 
AVIATION...LH

FXUS62 KILM 121828
AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
228 PM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Forecast PoPs have been reduced this afternoon into this evening
as various inhibiting factors are preventing widespread storms 
from forming. Models are trending cooler with the incoming 
Canadian airmass Monday night through Wednesday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

2) A modified Canadian airmass should bring cooler temperatures
beginning Tuesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge 
aloft will maintain chances for showers and thunderstorms 
through Sunday.

Forecast convective development today has been scaled back
significantly compared to what NBM and synoptic models were 
suggesting over the past 2-3 days. On a broad scale the culprit
may be subsidence from persistent offshore convection. On a 
more local scale, persistent mid level clouds inland, subsidence
behind a subtle shortwave lifting northward across North 
Carolina, or the lack of strongly convergent surface boundaries
could be to blame. Forecast PoPs through early evening have 
been scaled back to only 30-40 percent which is still higher 
than most of the recent CAMs suggest.

For any storms that do manage to develop this afternoon, the
airmass should still support locally heavy rain given slow cell
motion and anomalously high precipitable water values near 2.25
inches.

CAMs suggest new showers and thunderstorms may begin to develop
across the coastal waters around midnight. Mid level winds 
would tend to bring these northeastward where they could drop 
rain across portions of Brunswick and New Hanover counties late 
tonight into Sunday morning. 

Sunday's daytime seabreeze front may be the focus for additional
scattered showers and storms. The mid level flow will veer more
westerly on Sunday as a shortwave moves eastward across the 
Carolinas. Bulk shear should also increase to 15-20 kt which 
may lead to multicell storms redeveloping along boundaries like 
the seabreeze front. Drier conditions developing aloft inland 
during the afternoon should tend to reduce coverage of showers 
or storms there.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A modified Canadian airmass should bring cooler 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

The strongest Canadian high, 1030 mb, we've seen since last 
spring will move eastward across southern Quebec and New England
Monday through Tuesday, pushing a cold front southward. Models
are in excellent agreement showing the boundary will push 
across Cape Fear early Monday evening, racing southward past 
Myrtle Beach and Georgetown before midnight. 

Modified Canadian air will spread southwestward behind the
front Monday night, scouring out the excessive humidity and 
unseasonable warmth of the past week. Given the long path over 
75-85 degree water off the East Coast, this won't feel like a 
crisp fall airmass although it will be cooler and drier.

Forecast highs Tue-Thu should hold in the 80s, close to normal
for this time of year. The big improvement will be with
nighttime lows: models have continued to trend lower each run
and now show some potential for upper 50s in spots inland
Tuesday night. Dewpoints in the 50s and 60s will feel very
refreshing.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to develop
across this afternoon in an unseasonably warm and humid airmass.
Triggers for storm development should include the seabreeze 
front pushing inland from the beaches, and differential heating
along the edges of the persistent mid level cloud deck inland. 
Coverage should average 30-50 percent of the area this afternoon
which explains the PROB30 group for the coastal airports and 
the TEMPOs inland. Convection should diminish in coverage around
sunset.

VFR conditions overnight will likely become interrupted by low
stratus developing at KLBT and KFLO late tonight, mainly after
09z. This cloud cover should linger through 14-15z Sunday 
before mixing out into VFR conditions during the late morning. 
Along the coast, high-res models suggest marine convection 
streaming northeastward could affect the KILM airport after 
sunrise. Sunday's seabreeze front could also be a potential 
focus for new showers or storms affecting KMYR and KCRE mainly 
after 16z.

Extended Outlook... Scattered showers and thunderstorms 
bringing brief MVFR/IFR conditions are expected to continue 
into Saturday evening. Some showers are possible on Sunday, but 
coverage should be less than previous days. There is also a low 
potential for late night/early morning stratus or ground fog 
affecting KLBT and KFLO late Saturday night and again late 
Sunday night. VFR conditions should prevail Monday through 
Wednesday as a more stable and drier Canadian airmass builds in 
from the northeast.

&&

.MARINE...
Tonight through Thursday...Aside from anticipated waves of 
showers and thunderstorms developing late tonight into Sunday 
morning, then additional isolated showers/storms Sunday 
afternoon along the seabreeze front, marine weather conditions 
won't be too bad for the next couple of days. Synoptic winds 
from the southwest should average 10-15 knots with seas 
averaging 2-3 feet in a mixture of wind chop and a 9 second 
southeasterly swell.

Big changes should arrive Monday evening as a cold front sweeps
quickly across the area from the north. A surge of 
northeasterly winds should follow the the front, driven 
southward by the strongest Canadian high we've seen since last 
spring. Northeast winds 15-20 knots, occasionally reaching 25 
knots at times, should develop Monday night and persist through 
Wednesday. There's better than 50-50 chances wind/wave 
conditions will necessitate a Small Craft Advisory beginning 
Monday evening.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory until 1 PM EDT this afternoon for 
     NCZ107.
     Coastal Flood Advisory from 10 PM this evening to 1 AM EDT 
     Sunday for NCZ107.
SC...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

WHAT HAS CHANGED...TRA
KEY MESSAGES...TRA
DISCUSSION...TRA
AVIATION...TRA
MARINE...TRA

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
145 PM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Moderate Rip Current Risk all Local Beaches Today and Friday.
  Likely High Risk Returning by Tuesday Next Week

- Daily Heat Index up to 107 through Sunday

- Daily Afternoon & Evening Thunderstorms. Main Hazards: Locally Heavy
  Rain, Lightning & Gusty Winds Up to 40-50 mph

- Gusty coastal conditions and small craft advisory conditions
  developing Tuesday through Thursday next week

&&

.NEAR TERM /THROUGH TONIGHT/...
Main Highlights:

- Potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and localized flooding

- Summertime heat continues with heat index peaking in low 100s

Persistent and deep southwesterly flow prevails this afternoon and 
overnight between a dominant ridge and in incoming shortwave. The 
incoming disturbance will graze the region through tonight into 
Sunday morning as it deflects eastward off the stubborn ridge. A 
Gulf moisture tap, continues to stream a "premium grade" of deep 
moisture-laiden air across the area this afternoon. The same 
southwesterly flow delivering the moisture has already promoted 
early afternoon convection across the Suwannee Valley, which will 
continue to move east-northeastward around 15 mph while scattered 
showers will develop as diurnal instability increases through the 
mid to late afternoon. Convective trends through the rest of the 
afternoon will follow closely to what played out yesterday with 
stronger convection developing along the collision of mixed bag of 
boundary collisions consisting of the pinned Atlantic sea breeze, 
Gulf Breeze, St Johns River breeze, and amalgamating outflows. 

Highest concern with activity today will be the potential for 
concentrated flooding, mainly due to heavy rainfall rates that could 
push 4-5" per hour. Flood vulnerable areas will be those that are in 
poor drainage (urban) areas, low-lying, and at sites that received 
heavy rainfall within the last 24 hours. The I-95 corridor will be 
the main focus for the heavy rain/flood threat this afternoon where 
a 3-hr rainfall total greater than 1" is 70% and 3"+ at 30% for the 
NE FL portion of I-95. Despite the decent storm motion, the 
possibility of backbuilding will be possible along strong easterly 
outflows which may amplify flooding concerns. Additionally, enhance 
convergence along mesoscale boundary collisions may intensify 
updrafts producing strong thunderstorms capable of excessive 
lightning and strong outflow up to 50 mph due to water-loaded 
downdrafts.

Most of the convective allowing solutions depict weakening 
convection toward sunset this evening with potential for 
re-invigoration along leftover outflow as the aforementioned 
shortwave edges closer this evening. Divergence associated with this 
feature will be more likely to support evening convection through 
around midnight for portions of SE GA, mainly north of Waycross but 
cannot rule out a few attempts of as far south as I-10. After 
midnight activity will wind down and begin a recharge for another 
bout of convection Sunday.

Summertime heat continues under the influence of the upper ridge and 
will push readings into the low 90s through the rest of the 
afternoon and heat index into the low 100s. Under partly cloudy 
skies tonight temperatures will gradually cool to the low to mid 
70s.

&&

.SHORT TERM /SUNDAY THROUGH MONDAY NIGHT/...
Main Highlights This Period: (Sunday through Monday night)

- Daily Thunderstorm Potential Sunday and Monday, with a few strong 
storms possible, with gusty winds and heavy rainfall

A trough of low pressure will extend south across the southeastern 
US Sunday, with a high pressure ridge centered to the southeast 
extending across south FL. Between these features, the low level 
flow will from the southwest. The flow will be light enough for the 
east coast sea breeze to move inland to around I95. Convection will 
start inland Sunday late morning to early afternoon, then work east 
through the afternoon. The greatest chance for storms will be 
along the I95 corridor due to sea breeze interactions. 

The trough will dissipate Monday, as high pressure builds to the 
north northeast. The flow will remain light Monday, but will come 
more from the northeast to east. This will allow the east coast sea 
breeze to push well inland, so the convective max in the afternoon 
will be more toward the central part of the forecast area. Some 
drier will filter south into SE GA Monday, so higher convective 
chances expected for NE FL, than SE GA. 

Temperatures this period will remain above seasonal averages.

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Main Highlights This Period Tuesday through Saturday: 

- Daily Thunderstorms Potential

- Elevated Rip Current Risk 

Strong high pressure will build to the north northeast Tuesday 
through Wednesday night, an inverted trough develops just east of 
the region. The gradient between these two features will be pinched, 
leading to an elevated northeast flow. Tuesday and Wednesday will be 
gusty days along the coast, and across NE FL. Convection potential 
these two days will be greatest near the coastal trough, due to 
subsidence from the high. 

Inverted troughing will settle overhead Thursday through Saturday. 
Daily thunderstorm potential will continue due to diurnal heating 
and convergence associated with this trough. 

Near seasonal temperatures are forecast for this period.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH 18Z SUNDAY/...

Confidence in TSRA impacts remains high with TEMPO for all terminals 
between 18z-24z. Non-thunderstorm winds will be light southwest to 
west, with east coast sea breeze developing at SGJ and SSI now, 18z. 
Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 35 knots cannot be ruled out but hail 
is unlikely to develop with any strong thunderstorms that develop. 
Temporary visibility restrictions to IFR and possibly lower are 
expected due to torrential rainfall. Activity will diminish but 
lingering showers may continue through 00z before completely 
dissipating by 02-03z. There's a low chance that additional showers 
develop at SSI late this evening. 

Low stratus development and patchy fog may occur, especially inland 
during the predawn hours Sunday, mainly for VQQ and GNV; IFR stratus 
is possible. Winds will shift west-northwesterly on Sunday with most 
of the thunderstorm activity focusing across NE FL during the mid 
afternoon.

&&

.MARINE...

Weakening high pressure south of the area will maintain south to 
southwest winds and afternoon sea breezes through the rest of the 
weekend. Daily mid to late afternoon thunderstorms will move 
offshore, bringing locally strong wind gusts and frequent lightning 
at times. On Tuesday, a cold front will push south, sending a strong 
northeasterly wind surge through the local waters and elevating 
seas. Small craft advisory conditions are probable for the coastal 
waters starting Tuesday and may continue into Wednesday and 
possibly Thursday.

Rip Currents: Prevailing offshore winds (except for an afternoon 
sea breeze) and weak easterly swells will keep a low-end moderate 
risk of rip currents in effect the next couple of days. 
Strengthening northeast winds late Monday night into Tuesday will 
likely result in a high risk at all area beaches through at least 
Thursday as breakers build.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

A trough of low pressure will stretch across the southeastern US 
this weekend. High pressure will build to the northeast early next 
week, and strengthen through mid week. As this high builds, an 
inverted trough will develop east of the area. The gradient between 
these two features will result in elevated winds Tuesday through 
Thursday, especially at the coast. An inverted trough will settle 
overhead late in the week into the weekend. Daily thunderstorm 
chances are forecast, mainly in the afternoon and evening hours.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...

As far as rainfall today into tonight, areal amounts of around 0.2 
to 0.5 inches are forecast. Many areas may see less than that. 
However, model guidance shows some amounts of about 3 inches are 
possible in a few pockets mainly over the eastern zones, but also 
shown to be possible toward Alachua and Marion counties. As such, 
where these heavy rains occur today, temporary flooding is possible, 
especially in any poor drainage or urbanized areas.

&&

.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  91  73  92  73 /  60  40  10  10 
SSI  89  77  91  77 /  70  30  20  10 
JAX  91  74  92  75 /  80  40  40  10 
SGJ  90  75  91  76 /  60  30  40  20 
GNV  91  73  92  74 /  60  20  30  20 
OCF  92  74  92  75 /  60  20  50  10 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

FXUS65 KBOU 121810
AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1210 PM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Slightly cooler today, then unseasonably warm along the Front
  Range and I-25 Corridor Sunday. Isolated showers and storms, but
  some uptick over the mountains Sunday. 

- Unsettled pattern next week, with cooler weather arriving by
  Tuesday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 223 AM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

Cold front has pushed across northeast Colorado in these wee
morning hours. This will support cooler weather today, although 
high temperatures will still be near normal for this time of year.
A couple showers may linger over the northern plains early this 
morning, with redevelopment mainly over the mountains and Palmer 
Divide area this afternoon where airmass is less strongly capped. 
A few of these high based showers and storms could drift onto the 
adjacent plains as usual late in the afternoon/evening, but no 
significant precipitation is expected. 

We'll see low level moisture gradually return to the eastern
plains tonight, with areas of stratus likely developing 
along/east of a Limon to Sterling line. That does offer up some 
uncertainty for Sunday's high temperatures. Lee troughing indeed 
looks slow to develop, and thus the cooler and more moist boundary
layer conditions will likely persist more than most models 
advertise. While Denver and the I-25 Corridor is still shaping up
to be quite hot (lower 90s), somewhat cooler weather will likely 
hold over the eastern plains. While we've trimmed those 
temperatures from previous forecasts, further trimming is quite 
likely for the eastern plains due to the morning stratus and 
deeper moist boundary layer. Regarding convection, the mountains 
will see an uptick in convective coverage and intensity as another
monsoonal moisture plume pushes northeast into the state. 
Precipitable Water values increase to >150% of normal over the 
mountains, and thus a couple stronger storms could produce brief 
heavy rain. They will likely tend to weaken as they attempt to 
move off the higher terrain given locally drier airmass. At this 
time, the prospects of these tapping into the richer air over the
eastern plains also seems slim. 

For Monday, it still looks quite warm with more pronounced lee
troughing and downslope in west-southwest flow aloft. Regarding
convective potential, the plume of mid/upper level moisture shifts
across Colorado, but may end up being pushed too far south/east  
for higher shower/storm coverage. PoPs originating from model 
blends were still rather aggressive but wouldn't be surprised to 
see the higher coverage shift well southeast of the I-76 Corridor,
especially considering the eastward scouring of low level 
moisture ahead of the lee trough. 

Tuesday through Thursday is shaping up to have the highest
coverage of showers/storms for the week ahead. On Tuesday, the
monsoonal moisture plume is advertised to shift northward slightly
as an upper level trough digs into the western U.S. At the same
time, a more significant cold front will be pushing southward
across the plains, lending itself to a stronger low level upslope
component east of the Front Range. High temperatures are still
looking to cool into the 70s, with a 30-40% chance of highs 
holding below 70F on the plains. For Wednesday and Thursday, the 
forecast area would get into a more favorable location for weak 
synoptic scale lift as models are in better agreement with a weak 
shortwave lifting slowly east across the northern Great Basin into
Wyoming. We'll still need a weak front or two to help our upslope
in order to see higher shower/storm coverage, but trends have 
been in our favor here for light to locally moderate precipitation
amounts. Trends would then be for drier weather and near normal 
temperatures for later next week. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Sunday/...
Issued at 1134 AM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

Winds are beginning to settle into an easterly component across
the TAF sites early this afternoon. Expect wind speeds to see a
slight strengthening through the afternoon, but keep the easterly
component outside of any outflows or microbursts. Mid-level
moisture is expected to increase with showers and thunderstorms
already present across the higher elevations. This will increase
potential for afternoon/evening virga showers if things can hold
together coming off the higher terrain. A PROB30 has been
introduced to now include KDEN to account for this potential from
22Z to 1Z this afternoon. Microbursts/gusty outflows around 30kts
will be possible with any passing showers. Expecting winds to 
turn to the southeast then settle into drainage at KDEN/KAPA, with
KBJC remaining light and variable through the overnight hours. 

Slightly higher confidence in afternoon showers and maybe a weak
storm to pass across the TAF sites on Sunday. DCAPE looks slightly
more impressive and instability will be marginal for lightning
potential, but a PROB30 has been introduced at KDEN at 21Z, with
potential for a TEMPO to be considered for the evening hours in
the next TAF package. Gusts between 30-40kts will be possible with
any passing showers/storms Sunday afternoon/evening. 


&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$
